posts.title: Jellyfin stutters: Heavy processing
posts.excerpt: A follow-up to my transcoding post: Jellyfin stuttered on direct play too. The Pi's CPU was at 90%+ because qBittorrent and Bazarr were working through four seasons of a show at once.
posts.content:
In my last blog about [transcoding](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi), the stutter came down to the Pi converting a 4K Dolby Vision file it couldn't keep up with. Then it stuttered again, and this time nothing was being transcoded.

## Direct play, and still stuttering

By now I knew where to look first, so I opened the Jellyfin dashboard while it was stuttering. The session said "Direct playing". Nothing was being converted, the TV understood every part of the file and the Pi was just sending it over.

That ruled out everything from the last post. If the formats were fine and it still stuttered, then something else was keeping the Pi from sending the file fast enough.

## Look at the CPU

So I SSHed into the Pi and looked at what it was doing. The CPU usage was sitting at 90% or more, which is a lot for a Pi that is supposed to be just playing a file. If your stack runs in Docker, this shows which container is busy:

```bash
docker stats --no-stream
```

What I checked, in order:

- **Jellyfin session:** "Direct playing", so nothing was being converted. Ruled out.
- **CPU usage over SSH:** 90%+ busy, so the Pi was overloaded. The problem.
- **The busy apps:** Bazarr and qBittorrent, working through four seasons of Tulsa King at once. The cause.

## Who was using it

After digging around, it was Bazarr and qBittorrent. Seerr had been instructed to request a show with four seasons, Tulsa King, and had all of it queued up, and both of them were churning through all of it at once.

Seerr hadn't done anything wrong. The person who requested the show wanted all the seasons, so it asked for all four.

Everything in the stack lives on the same Pi, with the same four cores. qBittorrent is busy for as long as it has many active torrents, and Bazarr is busy for as long as it has a pile of episodes to look at. Jellyfin only needed a small share to direct play one file, but when two apps take most of the CPU, that share gets squeezed.

## The fix: one torrent at a time

I limited qBittorrent to one active torrent. The rest of the season now waits in the queue and gets worked on one after another, so there is much less going on at any moment. While playing a movie or show, the CPU is back to around 20 to 30%, and the stutter is gone.

In qBittorrent this is in the options, under BitTorrent and then Torrent Queueing. Set the maximum active torrents to 1. The labels might differ a little on your version.

It does mean a whole show takes longer to arrive, since the episodes are no longer downloading side by side.

## Watching it without SSH

This is the second time a stutter turned out to be the Pi working too hard, so a graph is easier than SSHing in every time. Beszel, the monitoring dashboard from the [last post](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi), shows the CPU chart too. Picking 12 or 24 hours shows what happened last night.

seo.metaTitle: Jellyfin Stuttering on Direct Play: Pi at 90% CPU - Tang Yetong
seo.metaDescription: Jellyfin stuttered even on direct play: the Raspberry Pi's CPU was at 90%+ from qBittorrent and Bazarr. Limiting qBittorrent to one active torrent fixed it.

posts.title: Jellyfin stutters: Transcoding
posts.excerpt: A follow-up to my arr stack post: how Jellyfin chooses between direct play and transcoding, why one TV stuttered on a 4K Dolby Vision film, and why the Raspberry Pi struggles.
posts.content:
At the end of my [arr stack post](/blog/raspberry-pi-media-server) I wrote that the TVs "can stream pretty smoothly most of the time" and that transcoding was outside the scope of the blog. This is the blog about the transcoding part, now that I've had the setup running for a few weeks.

I would say that transcoding is one of the biggest pain points of running the arr stack on a Raspberry Pi instead of a mini PC. To sum up transcoding: a video file is a bundle of a video format, one or more audio formats, and a container around them. A TV can only play the formats its hardware and app understand, and older TVs understand fewer of them. Jellyfin handles that in one of three ways:

The Pi struggles with video because it has no hardware video encoder, so the work lands on its CPU. Many mini PCs can hand this job to their graphics hardware, such as Intel's Quick Sync, so the same transcode barely registers.

This one is more of a notes post than a tutorial.

## The stutter

One night my parents put on *Fury* on the TV and it stuttered badly. Not a dropped frame here and there, but stop-start playback, as if the network was lagging. There were a few guesses as to why that was happening, for example the Ethernet being too slow for the 4K movie that was being streamed, transcoding, and so on, but it was only one movie, so I shrugged and moved on.

The next night *The Departed* did the same thing. The movie was borderline unwatchable, so I went looking.

## Look at the session, not the device

Jellyfin's dashboard shows every live session (Profile → Dashboard), and for each one it tells you whether it is "Direct playing" or transcoding, and why. Open it while the stutter is happening and the reason is usually right there in the live session information.

Here is what it showed for the TV (running the Jellyfin Android TV app 0.20.0):

- **Video:** 4K, Dolby Vision. Re-encoded, at about 12 frames per second, which is half of real time, so it stutters.
- **Audio:** Italian and English tracks, both Dolby Digital (AC3) 5.1. Converted to AAC, because the TV's app told Jellyfin it can't play AC3.

## Why one TV converts what another plays

The TV, or really the Jellyfin app running on it, tells Jellyfin which formats it can decode. Jellyfin checks every part of the file against that list. Whatever is on the list plays as it is, and whatever is missing gets converted. That is why the same file can direct play on one TV and transcode on another. The file doesn't change, the list does.

A file has several things in it: the container around everything, the video, the HDR on top of it, the audio and any subtitles. Each comes in several formats, and the TV has to understand each one it meets. Rough guide to how likely a TV is to play each without conversion:

- **Container:** MP4 is the most widely supported. MKV is used by most releases, and a TV that doesn't like it but is fine with what's inside only needs a direct stream, which is cheap.
- **Video:** H.264 (AVC) plays almost everywhere and is used by most 1080p releases. HEVC (H.265) plays on most modern TVs and is used by nearly every 4K release. AV1 only plays on recent devices and is still rare in releases.
- **HDR:** HDR10 is understood by most 4K TVs. Dolby Vision needs a TV and app that support it, otherwise the picture may have to be converted.
- **Audio:** AAC plays almost everywhere. AC3 (Dolby Digital) and E-AC3 (Dolby Digital Plus) play on most modern TVs, depending on the app and its settings. DTS is often missing on TVs. TrueHD and DTS-HD MA (lossless Blu-ray and 4K audio) usually need a soundbar or receiver.
- **Subtitles:** text ones such as SRT are drawn by the app, so there is nothing to convert. Image-based ones such as PGS (from Blu-rays) can force Jellyfin to burn them into the picture, which means re-encoding the video.

Which formats a TV can play depends on its chip and on the app running on it, so treat this as a rough guide. Dolby and DTS formats need licences, which is part of why cheaper and older TVs skip some of them.

So the cheap, easy combination is H.264 video with AAC audio, because nearly everything plays it. The risky one is the opposite end: Dolby Vision video with a Dolby or DTS audio track. Any one of those can be the thing a particular TV doesn't understand.

## What Radarr and Sonarr will actually download

Radarr (movies) and Sonarr (TV) know nothing about your TVs. They pick a release using the quality profile you give them, and a quality profile is mostly about resolution and source (for example 1080p Blu-ray or 2160p WEB-DL), with a size range. It says nothing about the video codec or the audio.

Custom formats are where you can be pickier. A custom format matches words in the release name, like x265, DV, Atmos or TrueHD, and gives it a score. Give a format a positive score to prefer it, or a negative one to avoid it. Without any, a 4K profile will happily grab whichever release ranks best for that quality, Dolby Vision and Dolby audio included. That is how a file like this one ended up on the Pi. Radarr and Sonarr also never convert anything. They download the release as it is.

The tags in a release name are what you can match on. Two made-up examples, taken apart:

- `2160p WEB-DL DV HDR DD5.1 H.265`: 4K, from a streaming service, Dolby Vision, HDR10, AC3 audio, HEVC video. Plays fine on a TV that handles Dolby Vision and Dolby audio. Otherwise the Pi has to convert it.
- `1080p WEB-DL AAC2.0 H.264`: Full HD, from a streaming service, AAC stereo, AVC video. Both formats are understood almost everywhere, so there is nothing for the Pi to convert.

## The audio was cheap, the video wasn't

Converting audio on its own is cheap, even for a Pi. If AC3 to AAC was the only thing happening, I'd never have noticed.

The expensive part was the video. The session showed the picture being re-encoded as well, and the Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware video encoder, so that happens in software on the CPU. The CPU can only manage 12 frames per second, which is half of real time.

Converting AC3 doesn't normally force a video re-encode, so the picture was probably being converted for its own reason, most likely the Dolby Vision or HDR handling. The dashboard lists the transcoding reason for each stream, so that is the place to confirm it. Either way, this is what happened to this file:

1. Audio: the TV can't play AC3, so the audio is converted to AAC. This is cheap, and the Pi copes.
2. Video: the 4K Dolby Vision picture is re-encoded on the CPU, only 12 fps, half of real time, so it falls behind.
3. Playback stutters.

That also explains why my other TV was fine. It direct-played *No Time to Die* because that file's audio is AAC, so there was nothing to convert.

## The fix: get the TV to accept AC3

If the TV plays AC3 as it is, nothing gets converted and the Pi never has to touch the video. All of this is in the TV's Jellyfin app, under Settings → Playback. Change one setting at a time and check the dashboard in between:

1. **Audio output:** set it to "Direct", not "Downmix to stereo". In downmix mode the app only accepts AAC, MP2 and MP3, so every Dolby file gets converted.
2. **Bitstream Dolby Digital audio:** turn it on, only if the TV or its soundbar handles Dolby Digital.
3. **Prefer FFmpeg for audio playback:** turn it on if it still converts after the first two, so the app decodes the audio itself.
4. **Then check:** play something for a minute. You want to see "Direct playing" in the session.

## The fallback: stop downloading Dolby Vision

If none of those settings work, then that TV can't play Dolby audio through this app, and I can't fix that from the Pi.

What I can do is change what comes in. In my case, the Dolby Vision release is the one where the video got re-encoded as well, so the fallback is to tell Radarr to avoid them. A 4K HDR10 or a 1080p release with the same audio would at worst cost the Pi an audio conversion.

## On the other hand, a TV streamer is coming

The house is getting a TV streamer, and the hope is that it takes some of the transcoding off the Pi and lets us play more video formats. That is mostly true, but not quite the way I first pictured it.

A streamer doesn't transcode anything on the Pi's behalf. What it does is run the Jellyfin app on better hardware, with a decoder that understands more formats (HEVC, Dolby Vision, Dolby Digital and so on) and usually the licences for them. When the app tells Jellyfin "I can play that", Jellyfin direct plays and the Pi just sends the file. So the conversion doesn't move to the streamer, it stops being needed.

There are catches. Streamers differ a lot, so check the specs for the formats from the guide above (HEVC, Dolby Vision, Dolby Digital and Digital Plus) before buying. The TV and soundbar still matter, since the streamer can decode Dolby Vision but the TV has to be able to show it, and lossless audio like TrueHD needs a soundbar or receiver to handle it. And whatever the streamer still can't play will still land on the Pi.

## A graph I can look at without opening a terminal

While I was at it, I wanted something nicer than SSH to see what the Pi was doing. I set up Beszel, a lightweight monitoring dashboard, and it showed the Pi straight away. It's at port 8090 on the Pi.

For "what happened last night", I pick 12 or 24 hours and look at the CPU and the disk charts.

Beszel can also send alerts when a threshold is crossed, but it needs a notification method such as email set up first, which I haven't done yet.

posts.title: Jellyfin: Avoiding subscriptions like the plague
posts.excerpt: How I set up an arr stack (Jellyfin, Radarr, Sonarr, Prowlarr and qBittorrent) with Docker Compose on a Raspberry Pi 5 8GB and a 1TB external hard drive.
posts.content:
A few weeks ago, I got tired of constantly asking my girlfriend to bring her iPad over to my house just to watch shows and movies. I have a TV at home, and constantly using the iPad never felt right.

I've never had a Netflix subscription, because I never knew if I could make it worth it. Would I really watch at least $20 of shows every month?

Then I stumbled onto some YouTube Shorts about setting up an *arr stack (Radarr, Sonarr, Jellyfin and friends), and it piqued my interest. It didn't look difficult or complicated, and it sounded like a fun weekend project.

This post is how I set it up, in the order that worked for me, with bits you can click on as you read.

## What I'm actually building

One Raspberry Pi runs all of the software, and the movies and series sit on an external hard drive. An arr stack is a set of self-hosted apps, most of them named Something-arr, that find, download and organise movies and TV shows for a media server. Nine pieces fit together here: Jellyfin (the media player), Seerr (the request website), qBittorrent (downloads the files), Radarr (movies), Sonarr (TV shows), Prowlarr (indexers), Bazarr (subtitles), FlareSolverr (gets Prowlarr past anti-bot checks) and Maintainerr (auto-deletes old media).

## Why isn't this just one plug-and-play app?

Nine containers is a lot of moving parts for "watch a movie". It makes sense when you think about it: each app does exactly one job, and they talk to each other through plain web addresses and API keys.

The upside is the flexibility to swap, update or switch off any single piece without touching the rest. You will feel the downside while setting everything up, though: more things to set up and keep updated. Debugging can also be a hassle.

## Picking the Pi, and everything else I needed

I went with the Raspberry Pi 5 8GB. The whole shopping list came to S$314.31, using a spare 1TB external hard drive I already had. It took about a week for everything to arrive, since some of the parts came from London.

## Setting it up, step by step

The core components are quite linear: flash the Pi, install Docker, mount the drive, launch the stack, then connect qBittorrent, Radarr, Sonarr, Prowlarr and Jellyfin. The optional apps (Seerr, Bazarr, FlareSolverr and Maintainerr) come in any time.

## My compose file, with your pick of containers

This is my stack written as a docker-compose file, with a builder that checks whether each container has what it depends on.

## Why every app mounts the same /data

Radarr and Sonarr don't copy a finished download into the library, they hardlink it: one file on disk, two names. That only works if both names live on the same mount.

## Getting the apps to talk to each other

Every connection screen asks for a host. The containers all share one Docker network, so the most reliable way is to use the container name. A reserved IP address for the Pi works as well.

## Things that usually go wrong

Nearly every problem I had comes down to a wrong address, a wrong path or a missing permission.

## Day to day

Day to day it's just: open Seerr, request something, wait. All of the TVs have the Jellyfin TV app installed, and can stream pretty smoothly most of the time. Transcoding is the exception, and I cover it in [Jellyfin stutters: Transcoding](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi). Pretty good convenience overall, and I think it's pretty worth it.

I only use this for content I'm legally entitled to download.

posts.title: Render Error: Cannot read property 'createClient' of null
posts.excerpt: Faced some issues tinkering with React Native's BLE library and trying to get it to work.
posts.content:
Faced some issues tinkering with React Native's BLE library and trying to get it to work. Was following this [repo](https://github.com/friyiajr/BLESampleExpo) and was faced with `Render Error: Cannot read property 'createClient' of null` while trying to load the app on Expo Go.

The app seems to be crashing on the line: `new BleManager()`, but loading the app on emulator works fine and crashes on Expo Go. Weird!

## Development Server

1) After playing around I finally got `BleManager()` to stop crashing after setting up the project to use a development build by running 

```bash
expo prebuild
```

2) Create a development build like so:

```bash
npx eas build --profile development
```

3) Scan the QR, install the app on your phone and open it. Then you will need to run the dev server for your development build:

```bash
yarn start --dev-client
```

The server should appear on the development build on your phone and then you can run your mobile app.

seo.metaTitle: Fix React Native BLE createClient Error - Tang Yetong
seo.metaDescription: Fix the React Native BLE "Cannot read property createClient of null" error that crashes BleManager in Expo Go, by switching to an Expo development build.

posts.title: How to contribute to Padawan Wallet
posts.excerpt: A quick summary of what the Padawan Wallet is, why it exists and how you can contribute to it!
posts.content:
A quick summary of what the [`Padawan Wallet`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/padawan-wallet) is, why it exists and how you can contribute to it!

## `Padawan Wallet`

The `Padawan Wallet` project started as a passion project by [@thunderbiscuit](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit) to play around with the newly created `BDK-Kotlin` library.
He envisioned a small android app that users can use to learn about bitcoin wallets.
Users will download the wallet, go through its tutorials and delete the app with full confidence that they can navigate other bitcoin wallets on the market. 

With the power of android, `BDK-Kotlin` and the bitcoin testnet network he created the first version of the `Padawan Wallet` as an open-source project.
After `Summer of Bitcoin` came around thunderbiscuit signed up as a mentor and brought in students to not only learn about bitcoin but to contribute to the project. 

The reason why this blog post exists is also because I worked on the project as part of my `Summer of Bitcoin` internship too. 
I brought the project from using fragments to Jetpack compose alongside the help many designers.

## How to contribute

As of writing this post the current `Padawan Wallet` project is undergoing a major shift to using the `Summer of bitcoin`
If you do want to help out or just check out the project codebase feel free to join the [discord server](https://discord.com/invite/hbMszDMP3X) where we all are!
You can drop thunderbiscuit or me and message on any questions you have about the codebase and we will be more than happy to reply.

The project uses Jetpack Compose to create the UI, and you can take a look at the design wireframe on our discord.
There are many open issues on the github, most of which are outdated and will be cleared once the project is moved to the Compose framework.

Of course, you can also use the project as inspiration on how to use the `BDK-Kotlin` library. 
The library is written in Rust, so do take a look if you are interested, it is also an open-source project!

Lastly, I just want to thank thunderbiscuit for teaching me about the bitcoin network and how to navigate the project codebase throughout the 3 months.

seo.metaTitle: How to Contribute to Padawan Wallet - Bitcoin Development
seo.metaDescription: Learn how to contribute to the Padawan Wallet project and get involved in Bitcoin development with BDK-Kotlin.

posts.title: Summer of Bitcoin 2022
posts.excerpt: This is the last week of the Summer of Bitcoin (SoB) 2022 internship and what a journey it has been.
posts.content:
This is the last week of the Summer of Bitcoin (SoB) 2022 internship and what a journey it has been.
When I was job hunting after being released from serving National Service in Singapore, I never thought that I would be taking on one that focused on Bitcoin.
Most of my friends and peers had negative impressions of Bitcoin and crypto in general, and I don't blame them, with all the shady business going on.
Personally though, I am neither for nor against Bitcoin.
I feel that in time bitcoin will fill out its niche, regardless whether its taking over the finance industry or not. 

I applied to numerous software engineer intern positions, though I never found SoB through my job hunting.
It was only after one of my friends sent me the link to SoB semi-jokingly and I thought it was pretty interesting. 
A fully remote intern position where I can do basically whatever I want? 
I thought this once a nice opportunity to learn something completely new to me, and to earn a nice chunk of change for myself too, so I signed up and got in almost immediately.

## Padawan Wallet
In the SoB internship you were either a developer or a designer, and every intern will have to pick a project and get the respective mentor to choose them over every other intern vying for that project.
It is a simple system, whoever catches the mentor's eyes the most will get the opportunity to work for them, and it encourages the interns to put in effort.
Since my programming background is mostly focused on Android, with web development being on the weak side and no knowledge on other up and coming languages like Rust, I went about to try and find some Android / Java projects to work on.
Luckily for me there just so happens to be 1 project that fits the bill, `Padawan Wallet`

The `Padawan Wallet` project started as a passion project by [@thunderbiscuit](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit) to play around with the newly created `BDK-Kotlin` library.
He envisioned a small android app that users can use to learn about bitcoin wallets.
Users will download the wallet, go through its tutorials and delete the app with full confidence that they can navigate other bitcoin wallets on the market. 

With the power of android, `BDK-Kotlin` and the bitcoin testnet network he created the first version of the `Padawan Wallet` as an open-source project.
After `Summer of Bitcoin` came around thunderbiscuit signed up as a mentor and brought in students to not only learn about bitcoin but to contribute to the project. 

The reason why this blog post exists is also because I worked on the project as part of my `Summer of Bitcoin` internship too. 
I brought the project from using fragments to Jetpack compose alongside the help many designers.

## How to contribute

As of writing this post the current `Padawan Wallet` project is undergoing a major shift to using the `Summer of bitcoin`
If you do want to help out or just check out the project codebase feel free to join the [discord server](https://discord.com/invite/hbMszDMP3X) where we all are!
You can drop thunderbiscuit or me and message on any questions you have about the codebase and we will be more than happy to reply.

The project uses Jetpack Compose to create the UI, and you can take a look at the design wireframe on our discord.
There are many open issues on the github, most of which are outdated and will be cleared once the project is moved to the Compose framework.

Of course, you can also use the project as inspiration on how to use the `BDK-Kotlin` library. 
The library is written in Rust, so do take a look if you are interested, it is also an open-source project!

Lastly, I just want to thank thunderbiscuit for teaching me about the bitcoin network and how to navigate the project codebase throughout the 3 months.

posts.title: Everything about my Internship at GovTech 2022 Summer
posts.excerpt: Everything about my 3 month internship at GovTech 2022 May - July.
posts.content:
Everything about my 3 month internship at GovTech 2022 May - July.

## Before

I applied to many places hoping that maybe I could score an internship (all the generic good places) with my limited experience in the industry. 
Most of my experience comes from working as a contract SWE at [RFCom Technologies](https://www.rfcom-tech.com/). 
Other than that I worked at [Travel Prologue](https://travelprologue.com/) as an intern.
I could get all these experiences from connections and they were a big hep in filling out my resume trying to find other jobs.

The person that hired me from Travel Prologue tried to contact me to come back and work for them again but I had changed my number during national service and I didn't know.
It was only long after that fact that I heard the news, so oops, my bad.

There were a few technical coding rounds that I tried and GovTech was the only one that responded back. 
Seeing that I was already a month or two into the job hunt I decided it was a decent place to intern at, and continued further down the interview path.
I actually had 1 more coding round from a finance company that I decided not to do, since I had to re-learn C++ to do it.

The interview was really simple except that fact that I forgot everything about databases, which they asked a few questions about. 
With that I got hired as an intern at GovTech for the _Personalise_ team for my summer before university starts.

## Start

Right when my internship started at GovTech some of the Covid restrictions got lifted, so more people could go to the work place.
I got pretty worried since I was juggling some other stuff (SoB) and going to the workplace means adding 2 hours of travel time to my weekdays. 
That would have been disastrous and I probably would have had to drop my other commitments.
Luckily for me GovTech still mostly practices work from home and I got let off the hook. 
Lucky.

A few days before I was supposed to report to work my "_Reporting Officer_" (RO) gave me the information on everything I had to install and do, which was pretty good.
The RO was one of the SWEs in the team and not the tech lead, so to be honest I was less stressed asking about small stuff. 
I went to take the company's macbook which was also my first time at the Sandcrawler building that DCube was in.
The place is really close to the mrt and the building itself is pretty cool, though not having a staff pass meant that you had to deal with security everytime you were waiting for someone to let you in.

I got introduced to everyone on the team, which included 4 SWEs, 1 data engineer, 1 designer and 1 person that dealt with the clients (I forgot the title).
The project itself is pretty huge actually, tons of submodules in the backend and a react frontend website was what I was introduced to. 
There are actually other components in the project but those were mostly for the AI and its implementation, which I was not really brought in to help with.

Everyone was a full-stack SWE which is a classic. 
I was given some very basic tasks as a start to get myself familiarized with the codebase, one of which was to change the website banner to the current year.
It didn't cross my mind to make the banner the _current year_, since the task told me to change it to _2022_. 
So I went ahead and pushed a very short 2 liner which still somehow had some peer review changes requested on it. 
After some time when the tech lead looked at the task he said just change the banner to the _current year_ and it clicked in my head that I messed up.
I wasn't thinking ahead and pushed stuff out without thinking through them, which I though was really bad, even though the consequences was pretty trivial.

## Middle

After getting used to the coding environment and all the schedules it was honestly pretty smooth sailing from there. The only problem I encountered was trying to find out which API I had to use and how to use it. Since the team is pretty small the amount of tech debt it had existing inside the code base is to be expected. The lack of documentation is also not a surprise so your choices really are to either memorize which piece of code is where, dig around until you find it, or to ask someone who does. 

This is around the time where I took on the task to handle data for the new Key Results (KR) that the team needed. Metrics such as the number of people who used a certain feature etc. needed to be recorded down so that we can keep track of it more closely. There were other issues such as the data collected being filled with actions that the developers had done. In the task I had to track several new metrics and clean up the dirty data, finally uploading all of them onto AWS CloudWatch.

seo.metaTitle: GovTech Singapore Internship Experience 2022 - Tang Yetong
seo.metaDescription: Complete breakdown of my 3-month software engineering internship at GovTech Singapore, including AWS CloudWatch work.

posts.title: Bumping RBF Enabled Transaction Fees using BDK-Kotlin
posts.excerpt: A quick guide on how to use the BDK-Kotlin 0.8.0 library to bump Replace-By-Fee(RBF) enabled transaction fees.
posts.content:
A quick guide on how to use the [`BDK-Kotlin 0.8.0`](https://github.com/bitcoindevkit/bdk-kotlin) library to bump Replace-By-Fee(RBF) enabled transaction fees. 
You can use the [`Padawan Wallet`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/padawan-wallet) and [`dev-kit`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/devkit-wallet/tree/simple-wallet) open-source projects as reference. 

## TxBuilder

With the `TxBuilder()` you can create the transaciton as per usual. 

```kotlin
var txBuilder = recipientList.fold(TxBuilder()) { builder, recipient ->
    builder.addRecipient(recipient.address, recipient.amount)
}
txBuilder = txBuilder.enableRbf()
txBuilder = txBuilder.feeRate(satPerVbyte = feeRate)
return txBuilder.finish(wallet)
```

As you can see we are just adding the recipient address and amount normally, while adding a `.enableRBF()` method.

posts.title: Custom electrum servers with the BDK-Kotlin wallet
posts.excerpt: A quick guide on how the user can change the wallet's electrum servers.
posts.content:
A quick guide on how the user can change the wallet's electrum servers.

## Why

Lets say, for example, you have promised your wallet users absolute anonymity when using it. 
Nobody should be able to come close to figuring out what you or your users are doing on the blockchain.
Perhaps you heard from a friend that the public blockchain indexing services are collecting the data of people who used it.

Although that is *highly* unlikely, the possibility that a public electrum server *can* conduct malicious activities might not sit well with everyone. 
To give an idea of what they *can* do :
 * Lie to you and tell you you have coins that you don't
 * Refuse to relay your spending transactions

It can't however :
 * Give you a fake receive address
 * Steal your wallet private keys

Electrum shares your wallet addresses with the server you are connected to so the server sees all your transactions. 

If you have your own electrum server set up, or just simply want to switch to different electrum addresses on the fly, it is trivially easy to accomplish using the [`BDK-Kotlin`](https://github.com/bitcoindevkit/bdk-kotlin) library.

## How

All you have to do is create a new `BlockchainConfig` object with the new electrum server URL, create the new `Blockchain` object off it, and finally sync the `Wallet` to the new `Blockchain`.

```
val newBlockchainConfig = BlockchainConfig.Electrum(ElectrumConfig(customElectrumURL, null, 5u, null, 10u))
val newBlockchain = Blockchain(blockchainConfig)
wallet.sync(newBlockchain)
```

And that's it! You are now connected to a new public electrum server, or you own custom run one. 

Do note, however, if the electrum server URL you have passed in is invalid (does not point to a server), the app might freeze. 
Do provide your own error handling either on the UI or the backend side.

seo.metaDescription: Why a public Electrum server can see all your wallet's transactions, and how to switch to your own server in a BDK-Kotlin wallet for better privacy.

## TxBuilder

With the `TxBuilder()` you can create the transaciton as per usual. 

```kotlin
var txBuilder = TxBuilder()
for (recipient in recipientList) {

}
txBuilder = txBuilder.feeRate(satPerVbyte = feeRate)
return txBuilder.finish(wallet)
```

You can write this piece of logic however you want, but to give an example of using scopes to read the `recipientList` data :

```kotlin 
val psbt = recipientList.fold(TxBuilder()) { builder, recipient ->
    builder.addRecipient(recipient.address, recipient.amount)
}.finish(wallet)
```

## Sign & Broadcast

After you have the `PSBT` object you can do whatever you want with it! Sign and broadcast with the `Wallet` and `Blockchain` object to send out the transaction.

posts.title: Creating Bitcoin transactions using BDK-Kotlin
posts.excerpt: A quick guide on how to use the BDK-Kotlin 0.7.0 library to create a simple 1 to 1 transaction.
posts.content:
A quick guide on how to use the BDK-Kotlin 0.7.0 library to create a simple 1 to 1 transaction, to transfer bitcoin (in our case testnet coins) from 1 person (you) to someone else. You can use the Padawan Wallet and dev-kit open-source projects as reference.

## TxBuilder

To create transactions using `BDK-Kotlin` is really simple, with the `TxBuilder()` class being really intuitive to use. To create a 1 to 1 transaction you will just have to call `TxBuilder()` with all the necessary information for a transaction to be broadcasted. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val psbt: PartiallySignedBitcoinTransaction = TxBuilder().addRecipient(recipient, amount).feeRate(satPerVbyte = fee_rate).finish(wallet)
```

The variables required to build a valid transactions are `recipient`, `amount` and `feeRate`. We will quickly go through each one since they are simple to understand.

`recipient: String` : This is the target address you want to send you `UTXO`s to. 

`amount: ULong` : This is the amount of `satoshi`s you want to send. 

`feeRate: Float` : This is the fees you want to spend to broadcast this transaction.

Finally you will have to call `finish(wallet: BDKWallet)` with the `Wallet` object you have created already. This returns a `PartiallySignedBitcoinTransaction`

## Signing a Transaction

> A Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (PSBT) is a Bitcoin standard that facilitates portability of unsigned transactions, which allows multiple parties to easily sign the same transaction. 
> This is most useful when multiple parties wish to add inputs to the same transaction. PSBT was introduced by BIP 174, and allows users to more easily sign transactions on a cold storage device and then broadcast the signed transaction from a device connected to the internet.

An advantage of having the `PartiallySignedBitcoinTransaction` object instead of having the library do the signing and broadcasting is that you can do many things with it outside of 1 to 1 transactions, such as adding [`multi-sig`](https://101blockchains.com/multisignature-wallets/) functionality in your wallet app. 

To continue where we left off, we will have to sign the transaction :

```kotlin
wallet.sign(psbt)
```

With this the `PartiallySignedBitcoinTransaction` (`PSBT`) is signed, and ready to be broadcast!

## Broadcasting a Transaction

```kotlin
blockchain.broadcast(signedPsbt)
val psbtTxid = signedPsbt.txid()
```

Calling the `broadcast()` method on the blockchain object will broadcast the `PSBT`. This is return a `GenericError` if anything goes wrong with the transaction, i.e. not having enough funds in your account. You can retrieve the transaction id (`txid`) by calling `txid()` on the `PSBT` object. 

With this you have created a 1 to 1 `PartiallySignedBitcoinTransaction`, signed and broadcasted it onto the blockchain for all to see!

posts.title: Creating a Testnet wallet using BDK-Kotlin
posts.excerpt: A quick guide on how to use the BDK-Kotlin 0.7.0 library to create a Bitcoin testnet wallet for your own testing purposes.
posts.content:
A quick guide on how to use the [`BDK-Kotlin 0.7.0`](https://github.com/bitcoindevkit/bdk-kotlin) library to create a Bitcoin testnet wallet for your own testing purposes. 
You can use the [`Padawan Wallet`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/padawan-wallet) and [`dev-kit`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/devkit-wallet/tree/simple-wallet) open-source projects as reference. 

## Wallet Creation

To create a wallet using `BDK-Kotlin` is really simple, with the `Wallet` class being really intuitive to use. To create a testnet wallet you will just have to call `Wallet()` with all the necessary information for a wallet to be created. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val wallet: Wallet = Wallet(descriptor = descriptor, network = Network.TESTNET, databaseConfig = databaseConfig)
```

The variables required to build a valid wallet are `descriptor`, `network` and `databaseConfig`. We will quickly go through each one since they are simple to understand.

`descriptor: String` : This is the wallet descriptor that tells the wallet how to generate addresses. 

`network: Network` : This is the network you want to connect to. In our case we want `Network.TESTNET` for testing purposes. 

`databaseConfig: DatabaseConfig` : This is the database configuration for the wallet to store its data.

Finally you will have to call `Wallet()` with all the necessary parameters. This returns a `Wallet` object.

## Wallet Recovery

To recover a wallet using `BDK-Kotlin` is also really simple. You will just have to call `Wallet()` with the mnemonic phrase instead of the descriptor. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val wallet: Wallet = Wallet(mnemonic = mnemonic, network = Network.TESTNET, databaseConfig = databaseConfig)
```

The variables required to recover a wallet are `mnemonic`, `network` and `databaseConfig`. We will quickly go through each one since they are simple to understand.

`mnemonic: String` : This is the mnemonic phrase that was used to create the wallet. 

`network: Network` : This is the network you want to connect to. In our case we want `Network.TESTNET` for testing purposes. 

`databaseConfig: DatabaseConfig` : This is the database configuration for the wallet to store its data.

Finally you will have to call `Wallet()` with all the necessary parameters. This returns a `Wallet` object.

## ExtendedKeyInfo

To get the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object from the wallet you will just have to call `getExtendedKeyInfo()` on the wallet object. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val extendedKeyInfo: ExtendedKeyInfo = wallet.getExtendedKeyInfo()
```

The `ExtendedKeyInfo` object contains all the information about the wallet, including the descriptor, network, and other metadata.

## Descriptor

To get the descriptor from the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object you will just have to call `descriptor` on the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val descriptor: String = extendedKeyInfo.descriptor
```

The descriptor is a string that tells the wallet how to generate addresses. It is used to create the wallet and can be used to recover the wallet.

## Mnemonic

To get the mnemonic from the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object you will just have to call `mnemonic` on the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object. As an example this is a snippet of the code used in `Padawan Wallet` :

```kotlin
val mnemonic: String = extendedKeyInfo.mnemonic
```

The mnemonic is a string that is used to recover the wallet. It is generated when the wallet is created and can be used to recover the wallet.

## Summary

To create a testnet wallet using `BDK-Kotlin` you will just have to call `Wallet()` with the descriptor, network, and database configuration. To recover a wallet you will just have to call `Wallet()` with the mnemonic phrase, network, and database configuration. The `ExtendedKeyInfo` object contains all the information about the wallet, including the descriptor and mnemonic.

Remember that to recover a wallet you just need the [descriptor](https://bitcoindevkit.org/descriptors/) to let the scripts know how to generate the addresses, hence after retrieving the `ExtendedKeyInfo` object it is easy to see that the rest of the code remains the same.
